title: Working as a Bartender
content:
The Role

Your job isn't just pouring drinks. It’s about flow, sharp timing, and reading the room. The guest sees confidence and control before they even taste the product. Your job is to deliver that — consistently.

You’re expected to: - Work clean, smart, and fast. - Know your drinks and how to talk about them. - Keep the bar, fridge, and storage dialled in. - Handle glassware properly and keep dish areas tight. - Know what’s on offer (food, cocktails, spirits, beers). - Be a team player. No attitude, no lone wolves.

title: Responsible Bartending
content:
We serve alcohol. That comes with responsibility. Help guests enjoy themselves without going sideways.

How: - Use measures. Know the ABV of what you’re serving. Eye-pouring is for cowboys and idiots. - Push water & softs. Hydration keeps the vibe alive. - Encourage food. Slows alcohol absorption. Also helps sales. - Be honest. If someone’s over the line, slow it down or cut them off — politely but firmly.

title: Alcohol, ID, and Measures
content:
Ethanol is the only alcohol we serve. It’s made by yeast fermenting sugars, typically from: - Cereal grains (wheat, barley, maize) - Fruits (grapes, apples, berries) - Sugarcane (rum) - Agave (tequila)

Yes, technically it’s fungus pee. Delicious.

🪪 CHALLENGE 25

If they look under 25, you ask for ID. Non-negotiable.

Accepted ID: - Passport - Driving Licence - PASS-accredited card

Serving alcohol to anyone under 18 is illegal — and your job’s on the line if you mess it up, offenders are subject to hefty fines and licenses are at risk! Remember that we can deny service and even entry without any reason given.

⚖️ WEIGHTS & MEASURES

Legal and consistent measures are the law. - Beer/Cider: Must be served in pints or halves. A pint = 95% liquid minimum. If someone wants a top-up, give it. - Wine: Sold in 125ml, 175ml, 250ml, or by bottle. - Spirits: 25ml or multiples (never free-poured unless it’s theatrical and measured).

There should be a measure notice visible behind the bar along with a document that states the premise license the venue operates under as well as a notice stating fire escape routes and the designated fire marshals.

title: Guest Interaction & Memory
content:
You’re not a robot. But you are a professional.

Traits that matter: - Welcoming: Be direct, warm, and aware of tone. Say hi like you mean it. - Personality: People remember good energy. Be real, be upbeat. - Knowledge: Know your spirits, your specs, your food menu. - Time Management: Multiservice = stacked drinks, smart batching, no dead time. - Awareness: Look up. Eye contact. Nod. Acknowledge. People hate being ignored. - Follow-up: “All good with the drink?” Easy win for service standards.

A bartender is part host, part technician, part performer.

🎭 SHOWMANSHIP

You’re on stage every shift. Guests clock your posture, movement, even how you shake or stir.

Keep it smooth, confident, and controlled. If flair’s your thing, go for it — but only if it doesn’t slow you down, sprays rum all over the place or decimates your glassware.

🧠 ANTICIPATION & MEMORY

Use memory like a weapon: - “That’s a Havana & coke, no ice, right?” - “Fancy that Tommy’s again?” - “Coming in hot with the Guinness!”

Small moves build massive loyalty. Remember orders, quirks, preferences — especially for regulars.

title: Hygiene & Setup
content:
Cleaning is part of the job, not a side quest. - Rotate glassware (hot at back, cold at front) - Handle glasses by stem/base - Don’t scratch, groom, or finger-lick while visible - Wash hands after handling cash, food, or weird stuff - Use blue plasters if cut; report it!

📦 STOCK CONTROL & WASTAGE

Every pour affects GP. Every spill costs the bar. (GP stands for Gross Product)

Things that must be logged: - Wastage/spillage - Kitchen transfers - Staff drinks - Complimentary drinks (must be manager-approved) - Voids

Giving away drinks = theft. It’s gross misconduct. End of. All discounts are to be approved by a manager or supervisor – what else would we be doing all day, right?

🧯 COMPLAINT HANDLING

Even if the guest is a tool, we must stay professional.

Follow the APOLOGISE Method: - Apologise - Praise (thank them for raising it) - Observe their mood/body language - Listen and empathise - Offer a solution - Go through next steps clearly - Instigate fix or fetch manager - Stay calm - Ensure they’re satisfied

SECTION 1: ROLE & CONDUCT As bartenders, we are the face of the venue. We do not just serve drinks — we host experiences for our guests.

Golden Rules: 1. Arrive 10 minutes early. Check your setup and team brief. 2. Maintain a clean, dry, and stocked station. 3. Engage with guests respectfully — attitude defines experience. 4. Never ignore a customer. Eye contact and acknowledgment go a long way. Meeting and greeting is key. 5. No personal devices during service. 6. No free-pouring. Ever. Use jiggers or CE marked measures. It is also illegal to underpour! 7. Be vigilant. ID checks are your legal responsibility (Challenge 25). 8. Rotate fridge stock (FIFO). Log wastage honestly. 9. Keep your station tidy — don’t wait to be asked.

“Every little action taken builds our reputation.”

SECTION 2: CLEANLINESS, HYGIENE & SETUP

Daily Standards: 1. Rotate glassware: hot glasses at the back, cold at the front 2. Handle glasses by stem or base — never by the rim 3. Keep the dispense area clean and dry 4. Use two cloths to polish: one damp, one dry 5. Wipe your station dry between rounds 6. All cutting boards and peelers must be cleaned between use 7. Hands are always in view — keep them clean and cut 8. Wash hands after handling money, bins, chemicals, etc.

Station Setup Checklist: 1. Spirits, beers, wine and mixer stock check 2. Ice wells full and dry underneath 3. Garnish prep: fresh fruit, herbs, twists 4. Soda gun tested, taps cleaned 5. Tools present: jigger, spoon, strainer, peeler, citrus press 6. Clean cloths ×3 (wet, dry, polish) 7. Bar top wiped, speed rail stocked, bins empty

title: Method & Technique
content:
Each cocktail has a method — and each method serves a purpose. Understanding when to shake, stir, build, or throw helps control texture, dilution, temperature, and clarity.

🎯 Method Breakdown

Shake – for aeration and emulsification Use when citrus, juice, cream, or egg white is present. → e.g. Daiquiri, Whiskey Sour, Espresso Martini

Dry Shake – no ice, just shake to foam Step one for sours with egg white or aquafaba. Always follow with a wet shake.

Hard Shake – short, sharp, aggressive Used for Sours or shaken drinks with body. Use large, cold ice cubes.

Stir – for control, clarity, and minimal dilution Used for spirit-only cocktails. → e.g. Martini, Negroni, Manhattan

Build – layered in-glass Long drinks where dilution is part of the drink. → e.g. G&T, Paloma, Tequila Highball

Throw – transfer between tins to chill without ice shock Used for delicate drinks like sherry or vermouth-led builds. → e.g. Adonis, Bamboo, Chrysanthemum

Lift – gently add soda or fizz Used to finish tall drinks — avoid over-agitation. No circular stirring.

Double Strain – when texture must be flawless Use a fine strainer to remove shards of ice, citrus pulp, or herbs.

title: Roundbuilding & Service Flow
content:
Service at a busy bar is about efficiency, rhythm, and calm under pressure. Roundbuilding is more than multitasking — it’s memory, motion, and presence.

    ✅ The Proven Roundbuilding Method:

  • Repeat the order back. Builds trust, helps memorise, and allows you to start visualising the build. 2. Sequence the drinks mentally. Start with pints (especially Guinness). Build long drinks next. Short stirred/shaken cocktails last. 3. Batch movement. Example: 4 x G&T? - Line up 4 glasses - Measure and pour all gin - Add all ice - Top all with tonic - Garnish all - Serve 4. Don’t rush the finish. Pour cleanly. Wipe drips. Place drinks with confidence. 5. Communicate during chaos. Call low stock, ask for glassware, and coordinate without shouting.

title: Core Cocktails to Know
content:
You should know these by heart. Recipes, ratios, method, and garnish — no cheat sheet.

Cocktail | Ingredients Summary | Method Old Fashioned | Bourbon, brown sugar, bitters, orange peel | Stirred Whiskey Sour | Whiskey, lemon, sugar, egg white or foamer, bitters | Dry + Wet Shake Negroni | Gin, Campari, sweet vermouth | Stirred Daiquiri | White rum, lime, sugar | Shake Tommy’s Margarita | Tequila, lime, agave | Shake Pisco Sour | Pisco, lemon, sugar, egg white, bitters | Dry + Wet Shake Amaretto Sour | Disaronno, lemon, rye, aquafaba, bitters | Shake Yuzu Negroni | Gin, Campari, vermouth, yuzu | Stirred Espresso Martini | Vodka, coffee, sugar — or Midnight Oil + Cynar (variant) | Shake Garden Fizz (AF) | Seedlip, elderflower, lemon, rosemary | Build + Lift

Every classic has a reason. Learn them, respect them, riff from them.

title: Product Knowledge Basics
content: You need to know: - The difference between bourbon and rye - What’s in a Negroni vs. a Boulevardier - What “dry shake” means - That gin isn’t just “like vodka with botanicals” - The “golden ratio” 1-2-1

    🌍 SPIRIT ORIGINS – QUICK REFERENCE

    Vodka: - Base: anything with starch (grain, potato, etc.) - Origin: Poland or Russia

    Gin: - Base: grain + botanicals - Key flavour: juniper - Origin: Netherlands/UK

    Rum: - Base: sugarcane/molasses - Origin: Caribbean - Note: French Rhum (e.g. Martinique) is elite

    Tequila: - Base: blue agave - Origin: Mexico (Jalisco + few others)

    Whisk(e)y: - Base: malted or unmalted grain - Spelling: - Whiskey = Irish - Whisky = Scotch and Japanese
